Kwame Nkrumah. Ghana's first president and a driving force behind African independence and pan-Africanism. He led Ghana to independence in 1957, making it the first sub-Saharan African colony to achieve self-rule, and championed a vision of continental unity that inspired liberation movements across Africa.

He led Ghana, then called the Gold Coast, to independence from Britain in 1957, becoming Africa's first sub-Saharan nation to break free from colonial rule and setting a template for other independence movements. He was a founder of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963, promoting pan-Africanism and continental solidarity against imperialism. He pursued ambitious industrialization and nation-building projects, building the Volta River hydroelectric dam and expanding education and infrastructure across Ghana.

He introduced a one-party socialist system and concentrated presidential power, eventually dissolving the legislature and ruling increasingly authoritatively. In 1966, while visiting China, he was overthrown in a military coup. He was exiled for a decade and died in Romania in 1972 without returning to Ghana. He spent his last years writing on African socialism and revolutionary theory, positioning himself as an ideological leader of the postcolonial struggle. Like Julius Nyerere and Haile Selassie, he championed pan-African unity, and Nelson Mandela later continued to advocate for the continental solidarity Nkrumah envisioned.
